In a joint status report released this morning, Apple said it is still waiting for Jon Prosser to provide additional documents and wants to re-depose Michael Ramacciotti, while both defendants are objecting to the way Apple is handling the case. Details below.

According to a joint status report filed with Judge James Donato, Apple, leaker Jon Prosser, and Michael Ramacciotti are increasingly at odds over who should be blamed for the delays in the trade secrets lawsuit Apple filed against the two men in July 2025.

A little background

As a refresher, shortly after unveiling iOS 26, Apple filed a trade secrets infringement lawsuit against Prosser and Ramacciotti over a Prosser video in which he leaked several details about the system, including the eventually-revealed major visual redesign known as Liquid Glass.

Apple alleges that Ramacciotti improperly obtained a development iPhone belonging to an employee, who was subsequently fired over the incident. Ramacciotti then conducted a FaceTime call with Prosser, showing him unreleased iOS features running on the device.

The case has had its share of drama since then. Because Prosser failed to respond to Apple's complaint within the deadline, the court clerk entered a default judgment against him (though Prosser has consistently denied ignoring the case).

Eight months later, the court agreed to vacate that default judgment, giving him another chance to formally answer the allegations.

Court filings show that Ramacciotti's side did respond to Apple's complaint and has largely cooperated with Apple's discovery requests.

However, since Prosser retained counsel and formally entered the case, the situation has shifted, with the three parties increasingly divided over who should bear responsibility for the alleged trade secret disclosures and the subsequent delays.

The latest joint status report

Returning to the latest status report, Apple said it wants Ramacciotti to update his interrogatory responses and sit for another deposition to address what it calls "inconsistencies between his testimony and that of Mr. Prosser."

Ramacciotti, however, says he will not agree to another deposition until Apple provides "a roadmap for resolving the claims against him, including exactly what Apple still needs from him (if anything)."

As for Prosser's side, Apple said it is "still waiting for him to produce a number of additional documents requested more than three months ago, including revenue reports and analytics for his YouTube channel, as well as records of relevant communications with third parties he referenced during his deposition."

Prosser pushed back, arguing that "the trade secrets at issue in this case apparently no longer are trade secrets, having entered the public domain." In other words, his argument appears to be that because Apple has already released iOS updates featuring Liquid Glass, the information at the heart of the lawsuit is now publicly available and therefore no longer qualifies as secret.

In the joint status report, Ramacciotti requested that the court hold a status conference this month, at which Apple would be required to explain what additional information it still needs from him. He also asked that Apple, within 30 days thereafter, either drop the claims against him or commit to taking the case to trial.

Apple, for its part, wants to continue the discovery process, including taking a second deposition of Ramacciotti and pursuing the documents he [Prosser] has yet to produce. Prosser contends that he has fulfilled the discovery obligations he agreed to undertake, and is objecting to Apple's continuing requests for additional materials.

If Judge Donato does not grant Ramacciotti's request for a status conference, the parties have proposed submitting another joint status report on December 2.
